items.title: fix(process): fail wait4 stores with EFAULT like Linux
items.body:
Fixes #220

## Summary

- The managed `wait4` stored the status word and the zeroed `rusage` with `PTRACE_POKETEXT`. A ptrace write ignores page protections, so a status pointer into read-only memory was written where Linux returns `-EFAULT`. An unmapped status or `rusage` pointer made the store fail, and the supervisor failed the domain.
- Both stores now go through the new `write_tracee_bytes` in `supervisor.rs`, a `process_vm_writev` of the whole buffer that honors the tracee's page protections. A short write counts as `-EFAULT`.
- Kernels built without `CONFIG_CROSS_MEMORY_ATTACH` return `ENOSYS` for `process_vm_writev` (for example minimal VM guest kernels), and a custom seccomp profile can return `EPERM`. If the first call fails with `ENOSYS`, `EPERM` or `EACCES`, the helper caches that and from then on uses the previous `PTRACE_PEEKDATA`/`PTRACE_POKEDATA` writes. A failed access (`EIO` or `EFAULT`) becomes `-EFAULT`, and `ESRCH` stays `ESRCH`. This path has reduced fidelity: an unmapped buffer still gives `-EFAULT`, but read-only memory is written, as before this change. The switch is announced once with `GINUX_SUPERVISOR_AUDIT: tracee-write=ptrace-fallback process_vm_writev=-38` (or `-1`).
- A store that faults makes `wait4` return `-EFAULT` to the caller, on the direct path and on the wakeup of a parked waiter. As in `kernel_wait4`, the child stays reaped, the status is stored before the `rusage`, and a faulting status skips the `rusage`. A new audit line `wait store fault caller=N reaped=M` records it.
- A status word that crosses a page boundary is written all or nothing, like the kernel's single 4-byte store. The part on the second page goes first; if the first page then faults, the second part gets its previous bytes back. A faulting `rusage` keeps the bytes before the fault, as `copy_to_user` does (measured natively).
- Any error other than `EFAULT` (for example `ESRCH` for a tracee that is gone) keeps the existing killed-task check and domain failure. A tracee killed during the store is still caught by the `PTRACE_SETREGS`/`PTRACE_SYSCALL` that follows.
- An unaligned `rusage` buffer no longer fails the domain. Linux accepts it, and so does `process_vm_writev`.
- The parent-tid store of `clone` (`store_tracee_tid`) keeps its unchecked ptrace write, now through the shared byte-merge helper `poke_tracee_bytes` (same per-word merge as before). The kernel ignores a failed `CLONE_PARENT_SETTID` store, so making it honor protections needs its own change.

Details and reproduction: #220.

## Changes

- `crates/ginux-init/src/supervisor.rs`: `write_tracee_bytes` with the cached ptrace fallback, `poke_tracee_bytes`, `fault_errno`, `syscall6`, `SYS_PROCESS_VM_WRITEV`, `EIO`, `EACCES`, `EFAULT`.
- `crates/ginux-init/src/main.rs`: `store_wait_results` (status, then `rusage`) and `store_tracee_status` (all-or-nothing status word) replace the ptrace stores. Both `wait4` store sites return `-EFAULT` on a fault. `store_tracee_tid` calls `poke_tracee_bytes`.
- `tests/fixtures/process-review-fixture.c`: scenarios `ro_status`, `bad_status`, `bad_rusage` and `straddle_status`. Each one reaps a child twice, once after it exited (`WNOHANG` poll) and once from a parked wait, and prints the result, the read-only word, the bytes around the faulting buffers, the status, the first `rusage` word and a second `wait4`.
- `scripts/test-process-native.py`: expected lines for these scenarios, the same as natively, with 20 repetitions each. A check that both rounds faulted and the second one parked, so both store sites are covered. New modes `<scenario>/vm-writev-enosys` and `<scenario>/vm-writev-eperm` for `wait_status`, `ro_status`, `bad_status` and `bad_rusage` run the same fixtures with a seccomp filter (installed with `ctypes`, no root needed) that fails `process_vm_writev` with `ENOSYS` or `EPERM`. They expect the fallback audit line, the same lines for `wait_status`, `bad_status` and `bad_rusage`, and the reduced-fidelity result for `ro_status` (the wait succeeds and the read-only word is written). The wrapped modes must report the fallback. In a plain mode the supervisor's own audit line decides which result applies: where it reports the fallback, for example on a kernel without `CONFIG_CROSS_MEMORY_ATTACH`, `ro_status` expects the reduced-fidelity result. `straddle_status` has no fallback mode: the page after its status word is unmapped, so the store already faults at the `PTRACE_PEEKTEXT` of that page, before any write.
- `Makefile`: the four scenarios added to `build-process-fixtures`.

## Testing

The four scenarios fail on `main`'s binary (64a3e3f7): `ro_status` with `wait=2` and `ro cell=10752` (the read-only word was written), the other three with a domain failure (`wait status store failed` or `wait rusage store failed`). With this change all four pass 20 of 20 runs in each of two full runs.

With `process_vm_writev` failing with `ENOSYS`, as on a kernel without `CONFIG_CROSS_MEMORY_ATTACH`, a first version of this change without the fallback failed `wait_status` with `GINUX_DOMAIN: failed reason=wait result store failed`. `main` passes there, because it only uses ptrace. With the fallback, the eight `/vm-writev-*` modes pass. The whole `make test-process-native` also passes when run under an `ENOSYS` filter and under an `EPERM` filter. In 200 further direct runs (50 per scenario, half of them pinned to one CPU) the blocking round parked every time.

| case | Linux (pid namespace) | `main` | this change |
|---|---|---|---|
| status in `.rodata` (`ro_status`) | `-14`, word untouched, `rusage` untouched | child pid, word = `10752` | `-14`, word untouched, `rusage` untouched |
| status unmapped (`bad_status`) | `-14`, then `ECHILD` | domain failure | `-14`, then `ECHILD` |
| `rusage` unmapped (`bad_rusage`) | `-14`, status `10752` stored | domain failure | `-14`, status `10752` stored |
| status crossing into an unmapped page (`straddle_status`) | `-14`, both bytes untouched | domain failure | `-14`, both bytes untouched |
| status crossing from `.rodata` into the writable page (manual probe) | `-14`, bytes on the writable page untouched | child pid, bytes on the writable page overwritten | `-14`, bytes on the writable page untouched |
| unaligned `rusage` (manual probe) | child pid, status stored | domain failure | child pid, status stored |
| kernel, wrapping and vsyscall addresses as status (manual probe) | `-14`, then `ECHILD` | not run | `-14`, then `ECHILD` |
| `ro_status` with `process_vm_writev` unavailable (fallback) | as above | child pid, word = `10752` | child pid, word = `10752` (reduced fidelity, as `main`) |
| the three manual probes above, fallback | as above | not run | `.rodata` crossing: child pid, both pages written (as `main`); unaligned `rusage`: as Linux; kernel addresses: as Linux |

| check | result |
|---|---|
| `cargo fmt --check`, `make check` (incl. clippy), `make test-unit`, `make build` | pass |
| `make test-process-native` (all scenarios incl. the four new ones, the eight `/vm-writev-*` modes and `legacy`), twice | pass |
| `make test-process-native` with `process_vm_writev` failing for the whole run, once with `ENOSYS`, once with `EPERM` | pass |
| `make test` (Rocky host VM suite, QEMU TCG, macOS arm64) | pass |

items.title: process: wait4 status and rusage stores ignore page protections (no EFAULT)
items.body:
## Summary

In `ginux process-native`, a managed `wait4` that reaps a child stores the status word and the zeroed `rusage` into the caller with `PTRACE_PEEKTEXT`/`PTRACE_POKETEXT` (`store_tracee_status` and `zero_tracee_rusage` in `crates/ginux-init/src/main.rs`, called from arm `61` of `supervise_process_native` and from `wake_waiters_for_child`). A ptrace write ignores page protections, and a failed one is treated as a supervision failure. Both differ from Linux, where `kernel_wait4` stores the status with `put_user` and `wait4` copies the `rusage` with `copy_to_user`, and a fault returns `-EFAULT` after the child is reaped:

- A status pointer into read-only memory is written: `wait4` returns the child pid and the read-only word now holds the status. Linux returns `-EFAULT` and leaves the memory untouched.
- An unmapped status or `rusage` pointer makes the ptrace store fail, and the supervisor fails the whole domain (`GINUX_DOMAIN: failed reason=wait status store failed`, or `wait rusage store failed`). Linux returns `-EFAULT` to the caller, and the domain keeps running.
- The same holds for a status word that crosses from a writable page into an unmapped one; Linux writes none of its bytes. An unaligned `rusage` buffer also fails the domain, while Linux accepts it.

Both store sites behave the same: the direct one (the child had already exited, also with `WNOHANG`) and the wakeup of a parked waiter.

glibc's `wait4`/`waitpid` pass the kernel result through, so a program sees `-1` with `errno == EFAULT` on Linux. Under `process-native` it either gets a success with read-only memory changed or never returns, because the domain is torn down.

## Expected

As on Linux: `wait4` returns `-EFAULT`, the child stays reaped (a second `wait4` for it returns `-ECHILD`), and memory the caller cannot write stays untouched. The status is stored before the `rusage`, so a valid status with a faulting `rusage` is still written, and a faulting status skips the `rusage`.

## Reproduction

The PR below adds the scenarios `ro_status`, `bad_status`, `bad_rusage` and `straddle_status` to `tests/fixtures/process-review-fixture.c` and `scripts/test-process-native.py`. Each one forks a child that exits with 42 and reaps it twice: first with a `WNOHANG` poll (the child has already exited), then with a blocking wait that parks while the child is still running. Each round passes these pointers:

| scenario | status pointer | rusage pointer |
|---|---|---|
| `ro_status` | an `int` in `.rodata` (read-only segment) | valid buffer |
| `bad_status` | `0x1000` (never mapped) | valid buffer |
| `bad_rusage` | valid `int` | `0x1000` |
| `straddle_status` | the last 2 bytes of the bss page, followed by an unmapped page | valid buffer |

The fixtures are static and `-nostdlib`, so they also run unchanged on Linux. Natively, in a new pid namespace (`unshare -Upfr --kill-child`), all four print `wait=-14` in both rounds, then `rewait=-10`, with the read-only word, the bytes around the faulting buffers and the skipped `rusage` untouched. In `bad_rusage` the status is still stored (`status=10752`).

With the PR checked out and `main`'s binary (64a3e3f7) built in a separate tree:

```
make build build-process-fixtures
python3 scripts/test-process-native.py <main>/target/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/release/ginux .artifacts/process target/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/release/process-native-fixture ro_status
```

All four scenarios fail on `main`:

| scenario | `main` | Linux |
|---|---|---|
| `ro_status` | `nohang wait=2`, `nohang ro cell=10752` (same in the blocking round), exit 0 | `wait=-14`, `ro cell=0` |
| `bad_status` | `GINUX_DOMAIN: failed reason=wait status store failed`, exit 1 | `wait=-14`, then `rewait=-10` |
| `bad_rusage` | `GINUX_DOMAIN: failed reason=wait rusage store failed`, exit 1 | `wait=-14`, `status=10752`, then `rewait=-10` |
| `straddle_status` | `GINUX_DOMAIN: failed reason=wait status store failed`, exit 1 | `wait=-14`, `edge=30583` (both bytes untouched) |

Output of `ro_status` on `main` (host pids elided, blocking round shortened):

```
GINUX_NATIVE_PROCESS_AUDIT: fork variant=fork host-result=... virtual-result=2
GINUX_NATIVE_PROCESS_AUDIT: sigchld queued parent=1 child=2
GINUX_NATIVE_PROCESS_AUDIT: sigchld delivered parent=1
GINUX_NATIVE_PROCESS_AUDIT: wait selector=2 virtual-result=2 status=42
nohang wait=2
nohang ro cell=10752
...
GINUX_NATIVE_PROCESS_AUDIT: wait parked caller=1 selector=3
GINUX_NATIVE_PROCESS_AUDIT: wait wakeup caller=1 child=3 status=42
...
blocking wait=3
blocking ro cell=10752
```

## Suggested fix

- Write both buffers with `process_vm_writev`, which honors the tracee's page protections the way the kernel's own copy to user memory does, and return `-EFAULT` to the caller when a store faults. Where `process_vm_writev` is unavailable (`ENOSYS` on kernels built without `CONFIG_CROSS_MEMORY_ATTACH`, or `EPERM` from a custom seccomp profile), fall back to the ptrace writes and at least return `-EFAULT` for unmapped buffers. The child stays reaped, as on Linux. Keep the existing killed-task and domain-failure handling for any other error.
- Keep the kernel's order: status first, then `rusage`, and skip the `rusage` when the status store faults. Make the 4-byte status store all or nothing when it crosses a page boundary.

A PR follows.

items.title: launch/native: sysinfo exposes host uptime, load, memory and process count (deny or emulate?)
items.body:
## Summary

In `ginux launch` and `ginux native`, `sysinfo` (99) is in the balanced task surface (`balanced_surface` in `crates/ginux-core/src/lib.rs`), so `decide_balanced` mediates it and it executes on the host. The workload receives the host's `struct sysinfo` unchanged: uptime, the three load averages, total, free, shared and buffer RAM, total and free swap, and the host-wide process count.

None of these values belong to the domain. The configuration of both lanes (`config/domain-gate5.toml`) sets `vcpus = 1` and `memory_mib = 256`, but `totalram` is the host's physical memory and `procs` counts every task on the host. This is host-topology information admitted for compatibility only.

`ginux process-native` does not pass it through: 99 is not in its contract, so `supervise_process_native` fails it with `-ENOSYS` before it executes, like every other entry it does not list.

Fixing this changes observable behaviour in either direction, so I would like your decision on the policy before opening a PR.

## Reproduction

A freestanding probe that calls `sysinfo` on a pattern-filled buffer and prints the fields, run under `main` (2489517e) in both lanes, as root:

```
GINUX_NATIVE_AUDIT: sequence=1 phase=entry syscall=99 action=mediate surface=task result=pending
GINUX_NATIVE_AUDIT: sequence=1 phase=exit result=0
sysinfo=0
uptime=<host uptime in seconds>
load1=<host load> load5=<host load> load15=<host load>
totalram=<host MemTotal> freeram=<host MemFree>
totalswap=<host SwapTotal> freeswap=<host SwapFree>
procs=<host process count>
```

The values are consistent with `/proc/uptime`, `/proc/loadavg` (the loads are scaled by 65536) and `/proc/meminfo` read on the host at the same time; `totalram` equals `MemTotal` in bytes. `launch` shows the same with `ginux: audit ... syscall=99 action=mediate surface=task`. Under `process-native` the probe gets `sysinfo=-38` and its buffer keeps the pattern.

An ordinary dynamically linked glibc program sees the same: `sysinfo()` succeeds with the host values, and `sysconf(_SC_PHYS_PAGES)` and `sysconf(_SC_AVPHYS_PAGES)`, which glibc derives from `sysinfo`, report the host's physical and available memory.

## Options

### A. Deny with `-ENOSYS`, as `process-native` does

Remove 99 from the task surface; `balanced_surface` then classifies it as `Denied`.

Consequence: glibc's `__get_phys_pages` and `__get_avphys_pages` ignore the `sysinfo` error and compute from the uninitialized `struct sysinfo` on the stack. `sysconf(_SC_PHYS_PAGES)` and `sysconf(_SC_AVPHYS_PAGES)` then return whatever the stack held, with `errno` `ENOSYS`. A probe that fills the stack with a byte before each call gave, in both lanes and with a current glibc (glibc 2.39 of Rocky 10 behaves the same way):

| stack fill | `sysconf(_SC_PHYS_PAGES)` | `sysconf(_SC_AVPHYS_PAGES)` |
|---|---|---|
| `0x00` | `0` | `0` |
| `0x11` | `6148914691236512545` | `6148914691236512545` |
| `0x7f` | `-8897841259083690871` | `-8897841259083690871` |

Python's `os.sysconf` gave values like `0` and `7752550405618130944` in the same setting. Programs that size buffers or caches from physical memory then see an arbitrary, possibly huge or negative, value. `process-native` returns the same `-ENOSYS` today, so glibc there takes the same path. With the Rocky userland, coreutils `sort` (which calls `sysinfo`) still produces the same output; `nproc`, `ls`, `gawk`, `find`, `du`, `tail` and `bash` do not call it.

### B. Emulate a successful `sysinfo` with deterministic values

`sysinfo` moves to the virtual-identity surface and never executes on the host. The supervisor writes a fixed `struct sysinfo` into the task's buffer and returns 0. Two variants:

- **Zero-filled**: every counter 0, `mem_unit = 1`. `sysconf(_SC_PHYS_PAGES)` and `sysconf(_SC_AVPHYS_PAGES)` return 0 with `errno` 0, the same in every run. This follows the rule `process-native` already applies to `wait4`'s `rusage` ("without usage accounting the honest bounded content is zeros").
- **Domain values**: `totalram` from `memory_mib`, zero loads, `procs = 1`, uptime since the domain start, no swap. This keeps `sysconf(_SC_PHYS_PAGES)` meaningful, but the README states that this path "does not implement resource quotas from the domain metadata", so a workload would be told about a limit that is not enforced.

With the zero-filled variant the measured results are:

| check in `launch` and `native` | `main` | B (zero-filled) |
|---|---|---|
| audit | `action=mediate surface=task` | `action=emulate surface=virtual-identity result=0` |
| `sysinfo(&buffer)` | `0`, `<host values>` | `0`, all counters 0, `mem_unit` 1 |
| `sysinfo(NULL)`, `sysinfo(<read-only buffer>)` | `-14`, `-14` | `-14`, `-14` (buffer unchanged) |
| `sysconf(_SC_PHYS_PAGES)` / `_SC_AVPHYS_PAGES` with the three stack fills | `<host pages>` | `0` / `0`, `errno` 0 |
| Rocky Bash native shell check | pass, no `sysinfo` call | pass, same audited sequence |

The buffer is written with `process_vm_writev`, which honors the task's page protections, so an unmapped or read-only buffer fails with `-EFAULT` as on Linux.

### Recommendation

I recommend B with the zero-filled struct: it is deterministic, it follows "virtualize, don't pass through" from #179, and it does not report an unenforced memory limit. A keeps today's `process-native` rule but leaves glibc's memory queries undefined. Either way the choice is yours. `process-native` would stay on `-ENOSYS` until you decide whether it should follow; I have kept it out of both variants.

## Scope

Other host-topology reads remain and are a separate question: `rseq` (334) registration makes the kernel write the host CPU number into the task's `rseq` area in all three lanes, and the same number is readable without any syscall through `rdtscp` and the vDSO `getcpu`, which ptrace cannot intercept.

Both variants are prepared with launch/native fixtures; I'll open the PR for whichever is chosen.

items.title: feat(console): support bounded polling of standard descriptors
items.body:
Programs using `poll` to wait for standard input or output readiness currently receive a policy denial in native execution. This adds a bounded allowance for descriptors 0–2 (plus ignored negative entries), with at most 16 entries and a timeout of 0–300 seconds. The supervisor validates the descriptor array before continuation; other descriptors, unreadable arrays, and unbounded waits remain denied.

Based directly on `main` at `0e06a986`. The launch fixture covers readiness, timeout limits, invalid pointers, descriptor restrictions, and closed descriptors.

Validation passed: `make check`, `make test-unit` (54 tests), release build, `test-launch`, `test-native-supervision`, and `test-process-native`.

items.title: balanced profile: read-only syscalls missing from the surface break common programs (getcwd, dup, chdir, uname, sleep, xattr reads)
items.body:
## Summary

I ran about 230 everyday commands from a Rocky Linux 10 root under `ginux launch` (balanced profile, `main` 2759c65f) and natively in the same namespace, as uid 1000 with `workdir = "/"`. Apart from the intended denials (fork/clone, pipes, execve, writable opens, network), the divergences below come from syscalls that are not in `balanced_surface` (`crates/ginux-core/src/lib.rs`) and therefore return `-ENOSYS`. None of them mutates the image or reaches the network; most are read-only or only affect the calling process. Ordered by how much they break:

| syscall(s) | what breaks under `ginux launch` | native |
|---|---|---|
| `getcwd` (79) | every `bash -c …` prints `shell-init: error retrieving current directory: getcwd: … Function not implemented`; bash `pwd` builtin fails; `python3 -c 'import json'` (any non-frozen import, because `sys.path[0] == ''` calls `os.getcwd()`) fails with `OSError: [Errno 38]` | works |
| `dup` (32), `dup2` (33), `dup3` (292) | every bash redirection (`read a < file`, `echo x >&2`) fails; `uniq -c FILE`, `shuf -n1 FILE` (freopen) and `dd if=FILE` fail. `fcntl(F_DUPFD)` (72) is already allowed without argument checks, so `os.dup(0)` works while `dup2(0, 5)` does not | works |
| `chdir` (80), `fchdir` (81) | `find … ` exits 1 with `Failed to restore initial working directory`; `df /` fails; `os.chdir` and bash `cd` fail | works |
| `uname` (63) | `uname -a` and `hostname` fail; `platform.system()`, `socket.gethostname()` fail | works |
| `clock_nanosleep` (230), `nanosleep` (35) | `sleep 0.1` fails (`cannot read realtime clock`); `tail -f` exits instead of blocking; `time.sleep` raises | works |
| `getxattr`/`lgetxattr`/`fgetxattr` (191–193), `listxattr` family (194–196) | `ls -l` prints `ls: <path>: Function not implemented` for every operand (exit 0) and loses the SELinux `.` marker; `os.listxattr` raises | works |
| `umask` (95), `times` (100) | the raw `-38` is returned by calls that cannot fail: `bash -c umask` prints `37777777732`; `os.umask` raises `OSError: [Errno 0]`; `os.times().elapsed` is negative | `0022`, positive |
| `statfs` (137), `fstatfs` (138) | `stat -f /`, `df`, `os.statvfs` fail; libselinux probes them in every glibc program (audit noise) | works |
| smaller: `getgroups` (115), `getpriority` (140), `sched_getaffinity` (204), `poll` (7), `pselect6` (270), `readlinkat` (267), `gettid` (186), `tgkill` (234, glibc `raise()`) | `id` shows only the gid, `nice` exits 125, `select.select` and `signal.raise_signal` fail | works |

Sample audit lines (each followed by the workload error above):

```
ginux: audit sequence=137 phase=entry syscall=79 action=deny result=-38
ginux: audit sequence=174 phase=entry syscall=33 action=deny result=-38
ginux: audit sequence=245 phase=entry syscall=230 action=deny result=-38
```

What already works identically: coreutils text tools on small files, `grep -r`, `sed`, `awk`, `tar -tf/-xOf`, `gzip -dc`, `sha256sum` on large files, `getent`, `locale`, `/proc/cpuinfo`/`meminfo`/`self/*`, `/dev/urandom`, bash builtins, and Python with `-I` for `random`, `hashlib`, `sqlite3` (in-memory), `tarfile`.

## Two related observations

- **`/proc` shows host pids.** `getpid()` returns the virtual 4242, but `/proc/self` points at the host pid and `/proc/self/status` shows the real `Pid`, `PPid` and a non-zero `TracerPid`; `os.path.exists('/proc/%d' % os.getpid())` is false.
- **Audit and workload stderr share fd 2 without line discipline,** so workload error messages are split mid-line by audit records (`cat: ginux: audit sequence=186 …` then `write errorginux: audit …`).

## Question

Which of these should the balanced profile admit, emulate (for example `uname` as virtual identity, `umask` as a virtual 022) or keep denied? I can send focused PRs with launch fixtures for whichever you choose. I have not changed the surface myself because each entry is a policy decision.

items.title: balanced profile: read/write/pread above their bounds fail with EPERM instead of a short transfer
items.body:
## Summary

`balanced_arguments_allowed` (`crates/ginux-core/src/lib.rs`) bounds the length of three mediated calls, and `launch` turns any violation into a hard `-1` (EPERM, `reason=invalid-arguments`):

| syscall | bound | check |
|---|---|---|
| read (0) | 1 MiB | `arg2 <= 1024 * 1024` |
| write (1) | 4096 bytes, fd 1/2 | `matches!(arg0, 1 \| 2) && arg2 <= 4096` |
| pread64 (17) | 1 MiB | `arg2 <= 1024 * 1024` |

Ordinary programs exceed these bounds all the time, because buffered I/O sizes its requests from `st_blksize` or the file size. On Linux a large request can legally return fewer bytes, and every common caller loops on that (glibc stdio, coreutils `full_write`, Python's `readall`/`write`). Under the balanced profile the request fails instead, so the program reports an I/O error.

## Reproduction

`ginux launch` against an extracted Rocky Linux 10 root, run as root with `workdir = "/"`, compared with the same program natively in the same namespace:

| program | native | `ginux launch` on `main` (2759c65f) |
|---|---|---|
| `cat` of a 108 KB file | full output | no output, `cat: write error: Operation not permitted`, exit 1 |
| `seq 2000` (first write is 8192 bytes) | full output | `seq: write error`, exit 1 |
| `python3 -S -c "import os; os.write(1, b'x'*4097)"` | 4097 bytes | `PermissionError: [Errno 1]` |
| `python3 -S -c "print(len(open('/usr/lib64/libc.so.6','rb').read()))"` (2.3 MB; `readall` asks for size + 1) | `2339896` | `PermissionError: [Errno 1] Operation not permitted` |

The boundary is exact: a 4096-byte write and a 1 MiB read succeed; 4097 bytes and 1 MiB + 1 fail. Audit lines:

```
ginux: audit sequence=185 phase=entry syscall=1 action=deny result=-1 reason=invalid-arguments
ginux: audit sequence=252 phase=entry syscall=0 action=deny result=-1 reason=invalid-arguments
```

`writev` (20) is bounded only by iovcnt (≤ 16), not bytes, so `os.writev(1, [b'y' * 100000])` succeeds while `write(1, 4097 bytes)` fails.

## Suggestion

The same choice as for getrandom in #163, where you recommended clamping: keep the per-call bounds, but shorten the length register to the bound before mediation instead of denying, so the caller sees a legal short transfer. Optionally give `writev` a total-byte bound for consistency. I have not implemented this because it changes observable syscall behaviour; I can send a PR (with launch fixtures for each call) if you want it.

items.title: balanced profile: the getrandom bound checks flags instead of buflen
items.body:
## Summary

`balanced_arguments_allowed` (`crates/ginux-core/src/lib.rs`) has `318 => arg2 <= 256`. For `getrandom(void *buf, size_t buflen, unsigned int flags)` on x86-64:

| register | argument |
|---|---|
| rdi / arg0 | buf |
| rsi / arg1 | buflen |
| rdx / arg2 | flags |

The check therefore bounds `flags`. Real flags (`GRND_NONBLOCK` 1, `GRND_RANDOM` 2, `GRND_INSECURE` 4) are always below 256, so the intended 256-byte bound never applies. `getrandom(buf, 1 << 20, 0)` is allowed today:

```rust
balanced_arguments_allowed(318, buf, 1 << 20, 0) // true
```

## Why this is a policy question, not a one-line fix

Moving the bound to `arg1` makes it effective for the first time, and a denied getrandom is fatal for some callers. glibc 2.36–2.40 (including 2.39 in Rocky Linux 10) has no vDSO getrandom. There, `arc4random_buf()` with more than 256 bytes issues the syscall directly and aborts the process (`Fatal glibc error: cannot get entropy for arc4random`) on any error except `ENOSYS`. I reproduced the abort by injecting `EPERM` into a 512-byte getrandom call (strace fault injection, glibc 2.44 fallback path). Normal startup is unaffected: glibc, Rust and Python seed with 8–32-byte requests, and `getentropy()` is limited to 256 bytes by its own API.

## Options

1. **Deny `buflen > 256`** (`318 => arg1 <= 256`): strict and a one-line change. Large `arc4random_buf` requests on glibc 2.36–2.40 then abort instead of reading.
2. **Clamp `buflen` to 256**: rewrite `rsi` to `min(rsi, 256)` before the mediated call, so the caller sees a short read. getrandom may return fewer bytes than requested, and glibc's `arc4random` and other careful callers loop. This keeps the bound and the compatibility, at the cost of a register rewrite in the native loops.
3. **Drop the bound**: the kernel already rejects unknown flags with `EINVAL`, and large getrandom requests are not a host mutation.

I can send a PR for whichever you prefer, with a unit test and a `test-launch` workload for the chosen behaviour.

Related note: on glibc ≥ 2.41 with kernel ≥ 6.11, getrandom is served from the vDSO and never enters the kernel, so ptrace does not see it and no bound can be enforced on that path.
